practice.q: According to the lecture, artificial intelligence is the ability of a computer program or a machine to ...
practice.why: The lecture defines AI as the ability of a computer program or a machine to think and learn.

practice.q: What does the course aim to build?
practice.why: The course sells itself as building an intelligent machine with mathematics and computing techniques.

practice.q: AI systems are described as working on their own without being ...
practice.why: The lecture stresses that AI works without being encoded with explicit commands.

practice.q: Which set of disciplines is listed as contributing to AI?
opts: Computer science, statistics, neuroscience, social science
practice.why: Slide 'Multidisciplinary in AI' lists computer science, statistics, neuroscience and social science.

probe.q: Which statement best matches the lecture's definition of AI?
opts: A machine that only stores and retrieves facts
A program or machine able to think and learn
A hardware accelerator for matrix maths
probe.why: AI is defined by the ability to think and learn, not by storage, rules or hardware.

probe.q: Early expert systems relied mostly on ...
probe.why: The slide states expert systems were built 'mostly with handcrafted rules'.

probe.q: Why did the field move from rule-based systems toward data-driven methods?
opts: Rules were too expensive to print
More variables, more compute and more data became available
Labelled data became illegal to collect
probe.why: The data-driven slide lists better models with more variables, more powerful RAM/CPU/GPU, and huge volumes of data.

topics.name: Machine Learning and the P-T-E framework

practice.q: Who said ML lets computers learn without explicit programming?
practice.why: Arthur Samuel (1959) gave that formulation; Mitchell (1998) added the <P,T,E> definition.

practice.q: What does P stand for in <P,T,E>?
practice.why: P is the performance measure on task T.

practice.q: What does E stand for?
practice.why: E is the experience the algorithm learns from.

practice.q: Which trio defines a learning task?
practice.why: A well-defined learning task is given by <P, T, E>.

probe.q: In Mitchell's framework, what does P measure?
opts: The size of the training set
How well the task T is performed
probe.why: P is the performance measure on the task, evaluated through experience E.

probe.q: A spam filter improves as users mark more messages as spam. What plays the role of E?
probe.why: Labelled examples are the experience; accuracy is P and filtering is T.

probe.q: Which element does 'predict tomorrow's temperature' correspond to?
probe.why: Predicting is the task T; accuracy of the prediction would be P.

topics.name: Deep learning and its relation to ML

practice.q: Deep learning is a class of what?
practice.why: Deep learning is a class of machine learning algorithms (Deng and Yu 2013).

practice.q: What does deep learning leverage?
practice.why: It leverages multiple layers to extract progressively higher-level features.

practice.q: What do the layers extract?
practice.why: Each layer extracts progressively higher-level features from the raw input.

practice.q: From what does deep learning extract features?
practice.why: The definition extracts features from raw input/output rather than curated summaries.

probe.q: In deep learning, the word 'deep' refers to ...
opts: the number of hidden layers between input and output
the depth of a decision tree
probe.why: 'Deep' refers to the number of hidden layers between input and output.

probe.q: Which ordering from broadest to narrowest is correct?
probe.why: Deep learning is a subfield of ML, which is a subfield of AI.

probe.q: A network with 20 hidden layers that learns features from raw pixels is best described as ...
probe.why: Many hidden layers plus learned features is the definition of deep learning.

practice.q: Which V covers data inconsistency and uncertainty?
practice.why: Veracity covers uncertainty due to inconsistency, incompleteness and ambiguity.

practice.q: Which V includes streaming and real-time data?
practice.why: Velocity covers batch, real-time and streaming data.

practice.q: Which V includes text, images, audio and video?
practice.why: Variety covers structured, semi-structured and unstructured data types.

practice.q: What scale is mentioned for volume?
practice.why: Volume is described as terabytes to exabytes to zettabytes.

probe.q: Data that must be processed in milliseconds as it arrives illustrates ...
probe.why: Millisecond-level response is the Velocity characteristic.

probe.q: Which four characteristics make up the 4V of big data?
probe.why: The slide lists Volume, Variety, Velocity and Veracity.

probe.q: Big data is defined as datasets so large and complex that they are hard to process with ...
probe.why: The definition points at on-hand database management tools and traditional processing applications.

topics.name: From expert systems to data-driven methods

practice.q: Which progression of models is mentioned?
opts: Rule-based to statistical to deep learning
practice.why: The slide shows rule-based -> statistical -> deep learning.

practice.q: Which computing resources are listed as drivers?
practice.why: More powerful RAM, CPU and GPU are named explicitly.

practice.q: Why is more data important?
opts: It reduces the need for labels
practice.why: Huge volumes of data allow analytics and discovery of valuable information.

practice.q: What weakness of handcrafted rule-based systems does the lecture highlight?
opts: They cannot be written in code
They do not scale to complex, variable real-world data
They need too much GPU memory
They cannot represent any knowledge at all
practice.why: The rhetorical question 'what might be the problem?' points at the brittleness of handcrafted rules, which is what motivated data-driven learning.

probe.q: Which factor is NOT listed as a driver of the data-driven turn?
opts: More variables to fit the data
More powerful RAM, CPU and GPU
probe.why: The slide lists models, hardware and data volume; cheap labelling is not among them.

probe.q: The lecture describes the evolution of models as ...
probe.why: Rule-based came first, then statistical methods, then deep learning.

probe.q: Expert systems are characterised in the lecture as ...
probe.why: The slide says 'Mostly with handcrafted rules!'

topics.name: AI tasks, methods and application areas

practice.q: Which is listed as an AI method?
practice.why: The task/method/area diagram puts machine learning and deep learning in the method band.

practice.q: Which is listed as an application area?
practice.why: Business, health, security, traffic and games are listed as application domains.

practice.q: Which task is mentioned?
practice.why: Translation is one of the language tasks in the diagram.

practice.q: Which is listed as an AI area rather than hardware?
practice.why: Image and video processing are task areas; the others are hardware or storage.

probe.q: Which task area converts speech into text?
probe.why: ASR converts speech to text; TTS does the reverse.

probe.q: Spam filtering is an example of ...
probe.why: The lecture lists spam filtering under text classification.

probe.q: Which group names AI application areas rather than hardware?
probe.why: The apps band lists business, health, security, traffic and games.

practice.q: What does regression predict?
practice.why: Regression applies when y is a continuous variable, e.g. price prediction.

practice.q: Which is a classification example?
practice.why: House-or-townhouse is a discrete label, so it is classification.

practice.q: What is the label type in classification?
practice.why: Classification predicts a discrete variable.

practice.q: Predicting a house price from size and lot size is which kind of task?
practice.why: Price is continuous, so the task is regression even with several features.

probe.q: Which task has a continuous output?
opts: Predicting whether an email is spam
probe.why: Temperature is a continuous value, so it is regression.

probe.q: Deciding whether a tumour is benign or malignant is ...
probe.why: Two discrete outcomes with labels is classification.

probe.q: The lecture distinguishes regression from classification by ...
opts: whether the label is continuous or discrete
probe.why: Regression: y in R (continuous). Classification: the label is discrete.

practice.q: Which three paradigms make up the lecture's machine learning taxonomy?
practice.why: The taxonomy slide splits ML into supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.

practice.q: Supervised learning requires ...
practice.why: Supervised learning is trained on labelled data to predict labels.

practice.q: Unsupervised learning aims to ...
opts: find structures or patterns in unlabeled data
practice.why: The goal is to find interesting structures or patterns without labels.

practice.q: Reinforcement learning learns from ...
practice.why: RL learns from rewards signalled for good actions, like dog training.

probe.q: Grouping customers into segments without any labels is ...
probe.why: No labels plus structure discovery is unsupervised learning (e.g. K-means).

probe.q: Which paradigm needs a reward signal instead of labelled answers?
probe.why: RL is driven by rewards, not by a labelled target for each input.

probe.q: The lecture compares reinforcement learning to ...
probe.why: The taxonomy slide uses 'Dog Training' as the metaphor for RL.
